source.title: Scaling Laws for Code: Every Programming Language Matters
source.authors: Jian Yang; Shawn Guo; Lin Jing; Wei Zhang; Ai-Shan Liu; Chuan Hao; Zhou-Jun Li; W. Zhao; Xiang-Long Liu; Wei-Feng Lv; Bryan Dai

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, but some equations and table/figure text are flattened or garbled.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits Chinchilla-style power laws to held-out code loss while varying model size and training tokens, using the same kind of scaling-law measurement in a code-pretraining setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports fitted loss-scaling relationships for individual programming languages and for translation settings. Its bilingual-mixture results and downstream generation evaluations are not, by themselves, tests of the parameter/token scaling claim; language-proportion allocation is a different allocation question and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study fits the Chinchilla form L(N,D)=A/N^αN+B/D^αD+L∞ to held-out code cross-entropy loss. It does this per programming language (420 runs: 0.1B–3.1B parameters × 2B–64B tokens × 7 languages) and for code-translation loss under different data-organisation strategies. That is the original method and measure, applied to code-LM pretraining. The fits bear on V1. The differences in fitted exponents across languages and strategies bear on V7. Table 3 (MultiPL-E Pass@1 at 0.5B–7B) bears on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that interpreted languages (Python) show larger scaling exponents than compiled ones (Rust), and that irreducible loss orders the languages C#<Java≈Rust<Go<TS<JS<Python. Add that parallel pairing gives favourable translation scaling and zero-shot transfer to unseen language pairs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Chinchilla-style power-law fits for code loss and translation loss, extending the scaling-law measurement to multilingual code; it does not reproduce the original natural-language datasets or experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling fits vary by programming language and by translation-training strategy (shuffled monolingual data versus explicit parallel pairing).

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed total training tokens, an allocation across programming languages guided by the scaling laws beats uniform allocation on average Pass@1 and BLEU.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed token budget, allocating tokens unevenly across programming languages using language-specific scaling and synergy estimates can improve average multilingual code performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing a second programming language beats repeating the target-language data (64B×2) for 6 of 7 targets; Python is slightly hurt by most auxiliary languages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under data scarcity, adding related-language data outperforms repeating the same-language data for code LM loss.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The main systematic sweeps cover a narrower range than several orders of magnitude. The text does not report uncertainty intervals for the fitted laws. Some equations and figure/table text are garbled or flattened, and the paper notes that its largest model and corpus are below state-of-the-art scales and that generalization to extreme scales remains unvalidated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. The bilingual synergy matrix and downstream generation results are not recorded as scaling-law rows because they do not test the versions' specified loss-scaling, compute-optimal parameter/token split, or downstream-predictability claims.

untested.parts: Scaling over several orders of magnitude: the sweeps span about 1.5 orders in N (0.1–3.1B) and in D (2–64B). Loss versus compute is not fitted. Fit quality and uncertainty are not reported.
No held-out extrapolation from small to large runs. The study only asserts that the fits can predict beyond the evaluated scales.
No compute-optimal N/D exponents. The text says optimal N:D ratios vary by language but gives no numbers.
No image or video models, fine-tuning or transfer scaling fits. The repeated-data comparison (Table 1) is not a scaling fit.
No fitted predictive relation between downstream score and scale or loss; only monotonic gains at four sizes.
Fitting method, parameter counting and schedule are not varied. Curvature away from a power law is not examined.

missing.what: Per-language fitted αN, αD and L∞ values (e.g. αN 0.221–0.845, αD 1.129–1.350, L∞ 0.288–0.566), garbled in the extracted text
Per-direction Chinchilla fit parameters (A, B, αN, αD) for the baseline across 42 translation directions, with widely varying exponents
MultiPL-E Pass@1 by language at 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B for baseline vs parallel pairing
Fit under the optimal language mix: αD*=0.6859, αN*=0.2186, L∞*=0.2025

record.verdict_notes: The abstract claims a 0.2B–14B, 1T-token scope, but the reported fits use ≤3.1B and ≤64B tokens, plus a 7B maximum for translation; no 14B result appears. The fitted αD values (~1.1–1.35) are far larger than Chinchilla's, unremarked by the authors. The equations are internally inconsistent (αa vs αz; β identical in Eq. 3 and Eq. 4). Rows r1–r20 were moved from V5 to V1 because code-LM pretraining is text-sequence LM pretraining, not another modality or regime.

versions.untested_parts: The paper varies model size and training tokens but does not independently establish loss scaling with compute while the other factors are not bottlenecks. The reported systematic sweeps cover 0.1B–3.1B parameters and 2B–64B tokens, not several orders of magnitude.
The paper says the fitted laws can inform predictions beyond the evaluated scales, but does not report a held-out test in which fits from small runs predict the losses of much larger runs.
The study optimizes how a fixed code-token budget is divided among programming languages. It does not test how parameter count and total token count should scale with compute.
Architecture details are held constant; depth, width, and other architecture choices are not compared at fixed parameter count.
The study tests code pretraining, including code-translation loss, but not image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer-learning regimes.
The paper reports downstream code-generation evaluations, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.
The paper reports differences among programming languages and training strategies, but does not systematically vary fitting choices or show that curves bend away from a single power law.

relationships.condition: Code-LM pretraining, 7 languages, 0.1B–3.1B params × 2B–64B tokens; translation loss 0.2B–7B
relationships.reason: Chinchilla-form power laws are fitted per language and per translation setting (r1–r10). Translation loss falls monotonically with size at fixed data (r11–r20).
relationships.display_finding: Chinchilla-form power laws fitted individual languages and translation settings, while translation loss decreased monotonically with model size at fixed data.

relationships.condition: Varying training data (programming language) and data organisation (shuffled vs parallel pairing)
relationships.reason: Fitted exponents and irreducible loss differ by language (r1–r7). The translation-loss αN shifts from 0.347 to 0.781 (or 6.404) across strategies (r8–r10).
relationships.display_finding: Exponents and irreducible loss differed across programming languages, while translation-loss αN changed from 0.347 to 0.781 or 6.404 across data-organization strategies.

relationships.condition: MultiPL-E Pass@1, 0.5B–7B, 1T tokens, both data strategies
relationships.reason: Based on text (Table 3, no row): average Pass@1 rises monotonically, 9.84→16.96→21.60→32.46 (baseline) and 10.12→33.79 (paired). No predictive fit.
relationships.display_finding: Average Pass@1 increased monotonically from 9.84 through 16.96 and 21.60 to 32.46 for baseline training and from 10.12 to 33.79 for paired training, without predictive fits.
